title: 401(k) vs. Roth IRA: Which One Should You Prioritize First?
description: The 'Order of Operations' for tax-efficient retirement saving.
content:
When saving for retirement, you have two main buckets: the 401(k) offered by your employer, and the IRA (Individual Retirement Account) you open yourself. Within those, you have 'Traditional' (Pre-Tax) and 'Roth' (Post-Tax) options. This matrix of choices often leads to paralysis. Do you take the tax break now, or later? Do you prioritize the match or the investment choices? The optimal strategy follows a specific 'Waterfall' to capture free money, minimize taxes, and maximize flexibility.

Key Takeaways

  • The Golden Rule: 401(k) Match > Roth IRA > Max 401(k). Never skip the match; it is a 100% ROI.
  • Tax Diversification: Having both Pre-Tax (401k) and Tax-Free (Roth) money in retirement allows you to manipulate your taxable income year-to-year.
  • Investment Quality: IRAs are usually better than 401(k)s because you can choose any ETF (low fees), whereas 401(k)s limit you to a specific menu (often high fees).
  • Liquidity: Roth IRA contributions can be withdrawn penalty-free anytime. 401(k) money is locked tight. The Roth doubles as a backup emergency fund.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 2025 limits are $23,500 for 401(k) and $7,000 for IRA. High earners can sometimes use the 'Mega Backdoor Roth' to put even more into the 401(k) if the plan allows. Understanding these caps helps you plan your cash flow.

The Priority Flowchart

Follow this sequence with every dollar of savings.

Step 1: The 401(k) Match

Action: Contribute exactly enough to get the full employer match (e.g., 5%).
Why: It is free money. A 100% instant return beats any tax advantage of an IRA.

Step 2: The Roth IRA

Action: Max this out ($7,000).
Why:
1. Tax-free growth forever.
2. No RMDs (Required Minimum Distributions).
3. Flexibility to withdraw principal.
4. Better investment options (Cheaper ETFs).

Step 3: The Rest of the 401(k)

Action: Go back to the 401(k) and fill up the remaining space ($23,500).
Why: It lowers your current year tax bill. If you are in the 24% bracket, every $1,000 you save only reduces your paycheck by $760.

Step 4: Taxable Brokerage

Only after steps 1-3 are full.

Roth vs. Traditional Decision

  1. Current Tax vs. Future Tax: If you think your tax rate is lower now than it will be in retirement, choose Roth. (Young people, lower earners).
  2. Peak Earnings: If you are in your peak earning years (35% bracket), choose Traditional. Take the tax break now.
  3. The 'Unknown' Hedge: We don't know future tax rates. Hedging by having 50% Pre-Tax and 50% Roth is a safe middle ground.
  4. The 5-Year Rule: Roth earnings are only tax-free if the account is 5 years old. Open one today with $1 just to start the clock.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I have both?

Yes! You can have a 401(k) AND a Roth IRA. You can even split your 401(k) contributions between Traditional and Roth if your employer allows it.

What if I earn too much for a Roth IRA?

Use the 'Backdoor Roth' strategy. Contribute to a Traditional IRA (non-deductible) and immediately convert it to Roth. This bypasses the income limit.

What if my 401(k) fees are terrible?

Only do the Match (Step 1). Then do Roth IRA (Step 2). If you still have money, you might prefer a Taxable Brokerage account over a high-fee 401(k) with bad funds.
